question: The word 'Jain' is derived from the term 'Jina'. What does 'Jina' mean?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Conqueror.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word Jain comes from Jina, meaning Conqueror; a Jina is a person who has conquered his own passions such as anger, pride, deceit and greed, and so broken the bonds of karma (जिन = विजेता, जैन = जिन के अनुयायी)

 

• The conquest meant here is purely inward: Jainism teaches that liberation comes from subduing the senses through severe self-discipline, not from any external power or divine grace.

 

• The followers of the Jinas are called Jains, so the very name of the religion points to its central ideal of self-conquest and personal effort.

 

• The Jain teachers who show others the path are called Tirthankaras, a separate title; the notes record that there were 24 of them in all.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The title 'Tirthankara' literally means 'ford-maker', one who builds a crossing over the ocean of rebirth (samsara) for others to follow.

 

• Mahavira was also called 'Nirgrantha' (free from all bonds), and Buddhist texts refer to him as Nigantha Nataputta, the Nigantha of the Jnatrika clan.

 

• Jainism rests on personal effort: a soul becomes a Jina by destroying its karmic matter, and no creator God can grant liberation.

 

NOTE

 

• Teacher (Option 1): 'Teacher' describes the function of a Tirthankara or acharya, who guides followers, but it is not the literal meaning of Jina, which stresses victory over the inner enemies rather than the act of teaching.

 

• Wanderer (Option 2): 'Wanderer' is closer to the Sanskrit term Parivrajaka, a general word for wandering ascetics of the sixth century BC; Jina has no connection with wandering and instead denotes conquest.

 

• Enlightened one (Option 4): 'Enlightened one' is the literal meaning of Buddha, derived from the root 'budh' (to awaken); the question tests whether a candidate mixes up the titles of the two sister religions.

question: How many Tirthankaras are believed to have existed in Jainism?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 24.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jain tradition holds that there were 24 Tirthankaras in all, beginning with Rishabhanatha (Adinatha) and ending with Mahavira, each appearing in the present half-cycle of time to restore the true path (24 तीर्थंकर)

 

• A Tirthankara is a soul who has attained Kevala Jnana (perfect knowledge) and then founds a four-fold community of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen to spread the doctrine.

 

• Historians accept only the last two, Parshvanath (23rd) and Mahavira (24th), as historical persons; the earlier ones belong to tradition and legend.

 

• Each Tirthankara is shown in sculpture with a distinct lanchhana (emblem) carved on the pedestal, which helps devotees tell nearly identical seated or standing figures apart.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jain tradition divides time into rising and falling half-cycles (utsarpini and avasarpini), and 24 Tirthankaras appear in each half-cycle.

 

• Several Tirthankaras attained liberation on Mount Sammed Shikhar (Parasnath hills) in Jharkhand, which is why it is the most sacred Jain pilgrimage hill.

 

• The Kalpasutra, attributed to Bhadrabahu, contains the biographies of the Tirthankaras, giving the most detail about Mahavira and Parshvanath.

 

NOTE

 

• 12 (Option 2): 12 is the number of Angas in the Jain canon (and of Upangas), not of Tirthankaras; a candidate who remembers the number twelve from the councils may wrongly choose it here.

 

• 22 (Option 3): 22 would omit the last two teachers, Parshvanath and Mahavira, who are the best known and the only ones generally accepted as historical, so the traditional count cannot stop at Neminatha, the 22nd.

 

• 27 (Option 4): 27 has no support in Jain tradition; the number of Tirthankaras is fixed at twenty-four, matching the 24 Tirthankaras shown in temple images and described in the Kalpasutra.

question: Who is regarded as the first Tirthankara of Jainism?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rishabhadev.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rishabhadev (also called Rishabhanatha or Adinatha) is the first Tirthankara of Jainism, and his emblem is the Bull; the notes call him the founder of the faith (ऋषभदेव — प्रथम तीर्थंकर, चिह्न बैल)

 

• Jain tradition describes him as a king of the earliest age who taught people agriculture, crafts and writing before renouncing the world, so he is the first teacher of the present half-cycle.

 

• The notes add that the Rigveda has references to two Tirthankaras, Rishabhadev and Aristanemi, which Jains cite to show the antiquity of their religion.

 

• His son Bahubali is remembered through the colossal Gomateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, which links the first Tirthankara with a major pilgrimage site.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Rishabhanatha is believed to have attained nirvana at Mount Kailash (Ashtapada), according to Jain tradition.

 

• His eldest son Bharata is regarded in Jain tradition as the first Chakravartin, a universal emperor, and India is said to be called Bharatavarsha after him.

 

• The names Adinatha (first lord) and Yugadideva are other titles of Rishabhanatha, and SSC options often use these alternate names.

 

NOTE

 

• Parshvanath (Option 1): Parshvanath was the 23rd Tirthankara, the son of King Ashvasena of Kashi, born at Varanasi; he is a historical figure who preceded Mahavira, but he stands near the end of the line rather than at its beginning.

 

• Sambhavnath (Option 3): Sambhavnath is the third Tirthankara of the traditional list, whose emblem is the horse; he comes after Rishabhadev and Ajitanatha, so he cannot be the first.

 

• Chandraprabha (Option 4): Chandraprabha is the eighth Tirthankara, whose emblem is the crescent moon; his name appears in the standard list but gives no claim to be first.

question: Which animal is the emblem (lanchhana) of the first Tirthankara, Rishabhanatha?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bull.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The emblem of Rishabhanatha (Rishabhadeva) is the Bull; it is carved on the pedestal of his images so that devotees can identify him among the 24 Tirthankaras (ऋषभनाथ का चिह्न — बैल)

 

• The system of lanchhanas exists because Tirthankara images look nearly identical, being shown either seated in meditation or standing in the kayotsarga posture.

 

• The notes pair the bull with the first Tirthankara, the serpent with Parshvanath (23rd) and the lion with Mahavira (24th), the three emblems most often asked in exams.

 

• In Jain tradition the bull also symbolises dharma, so it is a fitting sign for the first teacher of the faith.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara, has the elephant, and Sambhavanatha, the 3rd, has the horse as emblem.

 

• Shantinatha, the 16th Tirthankara, is identified by the deer, and Neminatha, the 22nd, by the conch.

 

• The bull (Nandi) is also the vehicle of Shiva in Hinduism, so the same animal carries different meanings in the two traditions.

 

NOTE

 

• Lion (Option 1): The lion is the emblem of Mahavira, the 24th and last Tirthankara; the notes give it for him, and it also connects with his title Vira (hero), so it belongs to the end of the series, not the beginning.

 

• Serpent (Option 2): The serpent hood spread over the head is the unmistakable emblem of Parshvanath, the 23rd Tirthankara, born at Varanasi, and it appears in his images at Mathura and Khajuraho.

 

• Elephant (Option 4): The elephant is the emblem of Ajitanatha, the 2nd Tirthankara, the immediate successor of Rishabhanatha; it is a common distractor because the 2nd Tirthankara follows the 1st.

question: Which Tirthankara was the son of King Ashvasena of Kashi and was born in Varanasi?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Parshvanath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Parshvanath, the 23rd Tirthankara, was the son of Ashvasena, king of Kashi, and was born in Varanasi; his emblem is the Serpent (पार्श्वनाथ — काशी नरेश अश्वसेन के पुत्र, सर्प चिह्न)

 

• He is regarded as a historical person who lived roughly 250 years before Mahavira, and he taught four vows (Chaturyama) to his followers.

 

• Mahavira's parents are said in the Jain texts to have been followers of Parshvanath, so Mahavira inherited and then reformed an existing community rather than founding a new one.

 

• Kashi was one of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, with Varanasi as its capital, so his birth in a royal family of Kashi places him firmly in the eastern Gangetic region.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Parasnath hills (Sammed Shikhar) in Jharkhand are named after Parshvanath, who is believed to have attained liberation there.

 

• The Uttaradhyayana Sutra records a dialogue between Kesi, a follower of Parshvanath, and Gautama, a disciple of Mahavira, resolving their differences on clothing and vows.

 

• A Jain temple at Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh is dedicated to Parshvanath and is mentioned in the notes under important Jain places.

 

NOTE

 

• Neminatha (Option 2): Neminatha (Aristanemi) was the 22nd Tirthankara, traditionally a cousin of Krishna of the Yadava family, with the conch as his emblem; he is connected with Dwarka and Mount Girnar rather than Kashi.

 

• Mahavira (Option 3): Mahavira was the 24th Tirthankara, born at Kundagrama near Vaishali to Siddhartha and Trishala; his father was a Jnatrika chief, not the king of Kashi.

 

• Rishabhadeva (Option 4): Rishabhadeva was the first Tirthankara, whose emblem is the bull and whose son Bahubali is honoured at Shravanabelagola; he belongs to the earliest age and not to the Kashi royal line.

question:
Match the Tirthankara with his emblem:

(a) Rishabhanatha  (i) Lion

(b) Parshvanath  (ii) Serpent

(c) Mahavira  (iii) Bull

(d) Neminatha  (iv) Conch
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rishabhanatha - Bull, Parshvanath - Serpent, Mahavira - Lion and Neminatha - Conch are the correct pairs, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (ऋषभ-बैल, पार्श्व-सर्प, महावीर-सिंह, नेमिनाथ-शंख)

 

• The notes supply the first three pairs directly: the bull for the first Tirthankara, the serpent for the 23rd and the lion for the 24th.

 

• Neminatha (Aristanemi), the 22nd Tirthankara, is identified by the conch (shankha), and the notes mention Aristanemi along with Rishabhadev as the two Tirthankaras known from the Rigveda.

 

• Such emblems are carved below the image because the Tirthankara figures are otherwise identical in posture and facial expression.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Parshvanath's image is usually shown with a canopy of serpent hoods (five, seven or eleven) above the head.

 

• Neminatha is connected with Mount Girnar in Gujarat, one of the holiest Jain hills, where he is said to have attained liberation.

 

• The lion emblem of Mahavira is linked to his name Mahavira (great hero) and to the Jain tradition that he was born in the Jnatrika kshatriya clan.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv (Option 1): This set swaps the bull and the lion, giving the lion to Rishabhanatha and the bull to Mahavira, so the first and last Tirthankaras are interchanged; the notes clearly give the bull to Rishabhanatha.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv (Option 3): This set gives the lion to Parshvanath and the serpent to Mahavira, though the serpent hood belongs to Parshvanath, the 23rd Tirthankara, born at Varanasi, and the lion to Mahavira.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 4): This set mismatches every pair, for example linking the serpent to Rishabhanatha and the bull to Parshvanath, and cannot be right when even two pairs are established by the notes.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Tirthankaras:

1. Rishabhanatha was the first Tirthankara.

2. Parshvanath was the 23rd Tirthankara.

3. Mahavira was the 23rd Tirthankara.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct answer is 1 and 2, as follows: Rishabhanatha is the first and Parshvanath the 23rd Tirthankara, while Mahavira is the 24th, so statement 3 is wrong (तीर्थंकर क्रम — ऋषभ 1, पार्श्व 23, महावीर 24)

 

• Mahavira came after Parshvanath and closed the line of the 24 Tirthankaras, which is why he is also called the last Tirthankara.

 

• Parshvanath preceded Mahavira by about 250 years according to Jain tradition, so the 23rd and 24th are teachers of two neighbouring generations, which explains why they are often confused.

 

• The serpent emblem belongs to the 23rd and the lion to the 24th, which gives a quick way to check any swap in the order.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahavira's followers were called Nirgranthas (free from bonds), while Parshvanath's followers were already present in Magadha when Mahavira began preaching.

 

• Mahavira added Brahmacharya to Parshvanath's four vows and insisted on complete renunciation of clothes, a point on which the later Digambara tradition rests.

 

• The 24 Tirthankaras are counted separately for each half-cycle of time, and the present cycle's 24th is Mahavira.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Only 2 and 3 includes the false statement 3, which makes Mahavira the 23rd Tirthankara, and it drops the true statement 1 about Rishabhanatha being first.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Only 1 and 3 keeps the true first statement but accepts statement 3, which is wrong because Mahavira is the 24th, and it leaves out the true statement 2 about Parshvanath.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): 1, 2 and 3 accepts all three statements, but statement 3 is false, since the 23rd Tirthankara was Parshvanath and Mahavira followed him as the 24th.

question: Aristanemi (Neminatha), the 22nd Tirthankara, is traditionally regarded as a cousin of which figure?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Krishna.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aristanemi (Neminatha), the 22nd Tirthankara, is traditionally regarded as a cousin of Krishna, since both belonged to the Yadava family (अरिष्टनेमि — 22वें तीर्थंकर, श्रीकृष्ण के चचेरे भाई)

 

• Jain tradition tells that on the day of his marriage he heard the cries of animals meant for the wedding feast, abandoned the ceremony and became an ascetic, which expresses the Jain emphasis on Ahimsa.

 

• The notes mention that the Rigveda gives information about two Tirthankaras, Rishabhadev and Aristanemi, so Aristanemi is the first Tirthankara after Rishabhadev to be tied to Vedic literature in the class notes.

 

• His emblem is the conch (shankha) and his place of liberation is Mount Girnar in Gujarat, a major Jain pilgrimage centre.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mount Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat has famous Jain temples dedicated to Neminatha.

 

• The Yadavas are the clan to which the Mahabharata and Puranas assign Krishna, who ruled at Dwarka.

 

• The Jain Harivamsa Purana retells the story of Krishna and Neminatha in the Jain version of the epic tradition.

 

• The Harivamsa Purana of the Jain writer Jinasena retells the Mahabharata story from the Jain viewpoint, with Krishna and Neminatha as cousins of the Yadava house.

 

NOTE

 

• Rama (Option 1): Rama belonged to the Ikshvaku line of Ayodhya and has no kinship with Neminatha, who is placed in the Yadava family; Jain tradition has its own separate Rama story.

 

• Gautama Buddha (Option 3): Gautama Buddha was a Shakya prince of Kapilavastu and a contemporary of Mahavira, born long after Neminatha, so he cannot be Neminatha's cousin.

 

• Arjuna (Option 4): Arjuna was a Pandava prince and a cousin of Krishna on his mother's side, but he is not linked with Neminatha; the tradition names Krishna alone as Neminatha's cousin.

question: Which additional vow did Mahavira add to the four vows (Chaturyama) preached by Parshvanath?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Brahmacharya.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Parshvanath preached four vows - Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya and Aparigraha - and Mahavira added Brahmacharya (celibacy or continence), thereby creating the five great vows (ब्रह्मचर्य — महावीर द्वारा जोड़ा गया पाँचवाँ व्रत)

 

• In Parshvanath's scheme, sexual restraint was treated as included in the vow of non-possession (Aparigraha); Mahavira made it a separate vow because of laxity in the community.

 

• The five together are the Panch Mahavrata, and the notes explain Brahmacharya as not leading an immoral life and observing continence.

 

• This addition shows that Mahavira reformed and tightened an older tradition rather than founding Jainism from scratch.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Parshvanath allowed monks an upper and lower garment, while Mahavira insisted on nudity for the strict monk, another point of difference.

 

• The Chaturyama Dharma of Parshvanath consisted of Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya and Aparigraha.

 

• The Uttaradhyayana Sutra preserves the discussion between the followers of the two Tirthankaras on why Mahavira changed the rules.

 

• Brahmacharya as a separate vow also explains why Jain nuns and monks live in separate groups, and why the four-fold sangha of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen was carefully regulated.

 

NOTE

 

• Ahimsa (Option 1): Ahimsa (non-violence) was already the first vow of Parshvanath's four, so it is not an addition and can only be a distractor for candidates who remember it as the most important vow.

 

• Satya (Option 2): Satya (truthfulness) was likewise included in Parshvanath's four vows, which means Mahavira simply continued it; it was not the vow he introduced.

 

• Asteya (Option 3): Asteya (non-stealing) was also one of the four original vows; it is inherited from the older tradition, not added by Mahavira.

question:
Assertion (A): Jainism is older than Mahavira.

Reason (R): Twenty-three Tirthankaras are believed to have preceded Mahavira, the 24th Tirthankara.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both A and R are true and R explains A: tradition holds that 23 Tirthankaras came before Mahavira, beginning with Rishabhanatha, so the religion obviously existed before him (जैन धर्म महावीर से प्राचीन — 23 पूर्ववर्ती तीर्थंकर)

 

• Mahavira is better described as a reformer and the last Tirthankara who systematised older teachings than as the founder of Jainism.

 

• Parshvanath, the 23rd Tirthankara, is the best-attested predecessor, and his followers were already organised when Mahavira began to teach.

 

• The class notes call Rishabhdev the founder of Jainism while giving Mahavira a special place, which matches this reading.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Jain community in Mahavira's time included followers of Parshvanath called the Pasavachchijja.

 

• Buddhist texts such as the Samannaphala Sutta mention the Nigantha leader Nataputta, i.e. Mahavira, and the four-fold restraint of the Niganthas.

 

• Rishabhanatha and Aristanemi are named in Vedic literature, according to the notes.

 

• Early Buddhist texts such as the Samannaphala Sutta refer to the Nigantha leader Nataputta, which shows that Mahavira's community was already a recognised rival of the Buddha's order.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): Saying R is not the explanation fails because the presence of 23 earlier Tirthankaras is exactly why Jainism cannot have begun with Mahavira; the reason directly supports the assertion.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): Saying R is true but A is false is wrong in the opposite direction: A is accepted by Jain tradition and by historians who regard Parshvanath as a real predecessor.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): Saying A is false and R true fails since the assertion that Jainism predates Mahavira is correct, as the reason itself shows.

question: Jamali, who is described in the notes as the first disciple of Mahavira, was related to him as his ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is son-in-law.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Jamali was the husband of Mahavira's daughter Anojja Priyadarshana, which makes him Mahavira's son-in-law; the notes name him the first disciple of Mahavira (जमाली — महावीर के दामाद एवं प्रथम शिष्य)

 

• Mahavira's wife was Yashoda and the notes record that the couple had a daughter called Anojja Priyadarshana, so the family connection to Jamali runs through the daughter's marriage.

 

• Jain tradition remembers Jamali later as the leader of the first schism (the doctrine that an action is complete only when finished), which shows disputes arose even during Mahavira's lifetime.

 

• The Jain family details come from the Kalpasutra and the Acaranga, which describe Mahavira's household before his renunciation at the age of 30.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahavira's chief disciples are called Ganadharas, and tradition counts eleven of them, headed by Indrabhuti Gautama.

 

• Mahavira's mother Trishala is said to have been the sister of Chetaka, the Licchavi chief of Vaishali.

 

• Mahavira organised his followers into a four-fold sangha of monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.

 

• Jain tradition states that Jamali later left Mahavira over a doctrinal quarrel, and he is counted as the first of the nihnavas, the schismatics of the Jain community.

 

NOTE

 

• son (Option 1): Son is wrong because the notes mention only a daughter of Mahavira, and no son appears in the standard account of his family; Jamali joined the family by marrying Priyadarshana.

 

• brother (Option 3): Brother is wrong because Jamali was not born into Siddhartha and Trishala's family; his tie to Mahavira came only through marriage to Mahavira's daughter.

 

• maternal uncle (Option 4): Maternal uncle is wrong because Jamali belonged to the generation after Mahavira as the husband of his daughter, while a maternal uncle would belong to the generation before him.

question: Mahavira was born in a royal family near which ancient city?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vaishali.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, the capital of the Vajji Mahajanapada in Bihar, which is why he is called Vaishalika (वैशाली — वज्जि महाजनपद की राजधानी)

 

• His father Siddhartha headed the Jnatrika kshatriya clan of Kundagrama, and his mother Trishala is linked by tradition with the Licchavi ruling house of Vaishali.

 

• The Vajji confederacy, with the Licchavis as its strongest clan, was one of the republican states of the sixth century BC, so Mahavira grew up in a non-monarchical political culture.

 

• The notes give two datings of his birth, 599 BC (traditional) and about 540 BC (modern), and note that he was born at Kundagrama in Bihar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Vaishali was also the venue of the Second Buddhist Council about a century after the Buddha's death.

 

• The Licchavis of Vaishali were later allied with the Gupta dynasty through the marriage of Chandragupta I with Kumaradevi.

 

• Kundagrama lies in the Vaishali district of north Bihar.

 

• Vaishali today lies in the Vaishali district of Bihar, where Basokund is identified with Kundagrama, and the Bihar Government celebrates Mahavira Jayanti there every year.

 

NOTE

 

• Taxila (Option 1): Taxila was the capital of Gandhara in the north-west and a great centre of learning, far from the Vajji territory, so it has no link with Mahavira's birth.

 

• Ujjain (Option 2): Ujjain was the capital of Avanti in the Malwa region of central India and is a different part of the country from the Magadha-Vajji area where Mahavira was born.

 

• Pataliputra (Option 3): Pataliputra was the later capital of Magadha, linked in this chapter with the First Jain Council, but it was not a city of Mahavira's birth and in his time Rajagriha was the Magadhan capital.

question: What was the childhood name of Mahavira?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vardhaman.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira's childhood name was Vardhaman, meaning 'one who grows', and the title Mahavira ('great hero') was given later after his spiritual victories (वर्धमान — महावीर का बचपन का नाम)

 

• He is also known by the titles Jina (conqueror) and Nirgrantha (free from bonds), which show how the later tradition honoured his austerity.

 

• The name Siddhartha is a trap: it was Mahavira's father's name, and it was also the personal name of Gautama Buddha, a contemporary teacher.

 

• The notes list 'Vardhaman' under childhood name, and 'Vaishalla' as another name for Mahavira, in the table of birth and family facts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Buddhist texts call Mahavira 'Nigantha Nataputta', that is, the Nigantha who belonged to the Nata (Jnatrika) clan.

 

• Mahavira's emblem is the lion, which suits the title 'Vira' (hero).

 

• Mahavira's age at death was 72 according to the notes.

 

• Mahavira Jayanti, the festival marking his birth, is celebrated on the 13th day of the bright half of Chaitra, and processions with the Jain flag are taken out on that day.

 

NOTE

 

• Siddhartha (Option 1): Siddhartha was the name of Mahavira's father, the head of the Jnatrika clan at Kundagrama, and also of the future Buddha; it is a different person from Vardhaman in the Jain account.

 

• Jamali (Option 3): Jamali was the husband of Mahavira's daughter and, as the notes tell, his first disciple, so he is a relative rather than another name for Mahavira.

 

• Kshama (Option 4): Kshama appears in the notes only in the name Kshama Sharman, the president of the Second Jain Council at Vallabhi, and has nothing to do with Mahavira's childhood name.

question: What were the names of Mahavira's parents?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Siddharth and Trishala.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira's father was Siddharth (Siddhartha), head of the Jnatrika clan at Kundagrama, and his mother was Trishala (सिद्धार्थ और त्रिशला — महावीर के माता-पिता)

 

• The notes call his father the King of Kundan gram and say that his mother was Trishala, and they list his wife as Yashoda.

 

• Trishala is said to have belonged to the Licchavi family of Vaishali, which linked Mahavira with the most powerful clan of the Vajji confederacy.

 

• Jain tradition says both parents were devotees of Parshvanath, so Mahavira was raised in an already Jain family.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Another name given to Trishala is Videhadinna in the Jain canon.

 

• Mahavira's elder brother was Nandivardhana, according to the Kalpasutra.

 

• Mahavira's own renunciation is placed at 30, after the death of his parents according to Jain tradition.

 

• Trishala is also called Priyakarini in some texts, and Jain tradition describes the sixteen dreams she saw before Mahavira's birth, which are a favourite subject of Jain painting.

 

NOTE

 

• Shuddhodana and Maya (Option 1): Shuddhodana and Maya (Mayadevi) were the parents of Gautama Buddha, a Shakya prince of Kapilavastu, so this pair belongs to Buddhism and not to the family of Mahavira.

 

• Ashvasena and Vama (Option 2): Ashvasena and Vama (Vamadevi) were the parents of Parshvanath, the 23rd Tirthankara of Kashi, so this pair belongs to Mahavira's predecessor rather than to Mahavira.

 

• Bimbisara and Chellana (Option 3): Bimbisara was the Haryanka king of Magadha who was Mahavira's contemporary, and Chellana was his queen, daughter of the Licchavi chief Chetaka; they are patrons connected with Jainism but not Mahavira's parents.

question: To which kshatriya clan did Mahavira belong?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Jnatrika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira belonged to the Jnatrika (Jantrika) kshatriya clan of Kundagrama (ज्ञात्रिक क्षत्रिय कुल — महावीर का वंश)

 

• Buddhist texts therefore call him Nataputta (son of the Nata or Jnatrika clan), and Pali texts call him Nigantha Nataputta.

 

• The Jnatrikas were a small clan allied with the Licchavis, the dominant clan of the Vajji confederacy; Mahavira's mother is traditionally connected with the Licchavi house.

 

• His father Siddhartha led the clan at Kundagrama near Vaishali, so Mahavira was a prince of a republican-style clan in north Bihar.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Gautama Buddha belonged to the Shakya clan of Kapilavastu.

 

• The Mallas ruled Kushinagar and Pava, where Buddha and Mahavira respectively died.

 

• The Vajji confederacy was one of the 16 Mahajanapadas with Vaishali as its capital.

 

• Pali texts such as the Digha Nikaya call the six rival teachers of the Buddha's time the Tirthikas, and name Nigantha Nataputta, that is Mahavira, as one of them.

 

NOTE

 

• Shakya (Option 2): The Shakya clan of Kapilavastu on the Nepal border was the clan of Gautama Buddha, not of Mahavira; the question deliberately contrasts the founders of the two religions.

 

• Licchavi (Option 3): The Licchavis dominated the Vajji confederacy at Vaishali and were related to Mahavira by marriage, but the notes name the Jnatrika clan as his own family.

 

• Malla (Option 4): The Mallas ruled the republican states of Kushinagar and Pava; Mahavira passed away among them at Pava, but he was not born into the Malla clan.

question: At what age did Mahavira leave his home in search of spiritual truth?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 30.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira left home at the age of 30 to become an ascetic, and the notes add that he then wandered for twelve years before attaining enlightenment (30 वर्ष की आयु में गृहत्याग)

 

• Gautama Buddha renounced the world at 29, so these two nearly equal ages are a standard trap in SSC questions.

 

• During the twelve years Mahavira practised severe penance, fasting and meditation, and in the Digambara tradition he gave up all clothing.

 

• After this the notes tell us he reached the highest knowledge, Kevala Gnana, in the 13th year of his penance, at about the age of 42.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Buddha's renunciation is called the Mahabhinishkramana and took place at 29, followed by about six years of search.

 

• Jain texts say Mahavira plucked out his hair in five handfuls at initiation (panchamushti loch).

 

• Mahavira then preached for 30 years until he died at 72.

 

• Jain texts say he plucked out his hair in five handfuls (panchamushti loch) at initiation, and this ritual of pulling out hair is still followed by Jain monks and nuns today.

 

NOTE

 

• 25 (Option 1): 25 is not Mahavira's age of renunciation and does not match the 30-plus-12-plus-30 sequence in the notes that gives a lifespan of 72 years.

 

• 35 (Option 2): 35 is wrong because by 35 Mahavira had already been an ascetic for about five years and was still in the middle of his twelve-year search.

 

• 40 (Option 3): 40 is wrong because Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana at about 42 after twelve years of wandering, so he was already well advanced in penance at 40.

question:
Match the following about Mahavira:

(a) Father  (i) Yashoda

(b) Mother  (ii) Vardhaman

(c) Wife  (iii) Siddhartha

(d) Childhood name  (iv) Trishala
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Father - Siddhartha, Mother - Trishala, Wife - Yashoda and Childhood name - Vardhaman give a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii (पिता सिद्धार्थ, माता त्रिशला, पत्नी यशोदा, बचपन का नाम वर्धमान)

 

• The notes tabulate these points under 'Birth and Family' as father, mother, wife, daughter, clan and childhood name.

 

• His daughter Anojja Priyadarshana married Jamali, who became Mahavira's first disciple, so the family is linked to the early sangha.

 

• All these relationships belong to Mahavira's life before his renunciation at the age of 30.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Siddhartha is also the name of the Buddha, which is a common source of confusion.

 

• Tradition adds that Mahavira's elder brother was Nandivardhana.

 

• Yashoda should not be confused with Yashodhara, the wife of Gautama Buddha.

 

• The Jain tradition counts Nandivardhana as Mahavira's elder brother, and the Kalpasutra says that Mahavira renounced the world only after receiving permission from his elder brother.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 2): This set swaps father and mother and also wife and childhood name, so every pair is wrong; Siddhartha is the father and Trishala the mother.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 3): This set makes Trishala the wife and Yashoda the mother, which reverses the real relationships of Mahavira's family given in the notes.

 

• a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii (Option 4): This set pairs the father with the childhood name Vardhaman and the childhood name with Siddhartha, so it confuses a person's name with the name of the child.

question: For how many years did Mahavira wander as an ascetic before attaining Kevala Jnana (the highest knowledge)?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Twelve.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira wandered for twelve years after leaving home and attained Kevala Jnana in the 13th year of his penance (12 वर्ष की तपस्या के बाद केवल ज्ञान)

 

• Kevala Jnana is perfect, infinite knowledge that arises only when the soul is free from karmic matter, and the notes call it the highest spiritual knowledge.

 

• After this he came to be called Jina (conqueror) and Mahavira, and he began to preach his doctrine.

 

• He then preached for 30 years, so the thirty is the length of his teaching career and not of his earlier penance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Buddha attained enlightenment after about six years of search, which makes six a common distractor.

 

• Mahavira was about 42 when he gained Kevala Jnana.

 

• Jain texts say he practised meditation and fasts for months at a time during these wanderings in Bihar and Bengal.

 

• Jain texts say that during these twelve years Mahavira meditated for long periods in forests and workshops of potters, and suffered attacks, and his wandering is traced across Anga, Magadha and Videha.

 

NOTE

 

• Six (Option 1): Six years is roughly the period of Gautama Buddha's quest before enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, so it comes from Buddhism and not from the Jain account of Mahavira.

 

• Twenty (Option 2): Twenty years is not stated in the notes and does not fit the age sequence of leaving home at 30 and reaching enlightenment at about 42.

 

• Thirty (Option 4): Thirty years is the length of Mahavira's preaching career after Kevala Jnana, ending with his death at 72, and not the length of the penance before it.

question: On the banks of which river did Mahavira attain Kevala Jnana?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rijupalika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana near the Rijupalika (Riju Palika) river, under a Sal tree at Jimbhikagrama in Bihar (ऋजुपालिका नदी, साल वृक्ष, जृम्भिकग्राम)

 

• This happened in the 13th year of his penance and made him a Jina and an omniscient teacher.

 

• The Buddha attained enlightenment under a Pipal (Bodhi) tree at Bodh Gaya near the Niranjana (Falgu) river; the two river-and-tree combinations are a standard comparison.

 

• The notes record the river, the tree and the village together, so each of these three identifiers can appear as a separate question.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jimbhikagrama is traditionally identified with a village in the Jamui district of Bihar.

 

• Buddha's first sermon was at Sarnath, while Mahavira's first sermon is said to have been at Vipulachala hill near Rajagriha.

 

• Buddha died at Kushinagar and Mahavira at Pava.

 

• After the Kevala Jnana at Jrimbhikagrama, Mahavira delivered his first sermon, and the tradition says that eleven Brahmin scholars led by Indrabhuti Gautama became his chief disciples, the Ganadharas.

 

NOTE

 

• Niranjana (Option 2): The Niranjana (Falgu) river flows by Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, so it is the Buddhist counterpart of the Rijupalika.

 

• Son (Option 3): The Son (Sona) river joins the Ganga near Patna and is an important river of Magadha, but it is not tied to Mahavira's Kevala Jnana in the notes.

 

• Gandak (Option 4): The Gandak is a Himalayan river that flows near Vaishali and joins the Ganga opposite Patna, and it plays no part in the story of Mahavira's enlightenment.

question:
Consider the following statements about Mahavira:

1. He preached his doctrines for 30 years.

2. He died at the age of 72 at Pava near Rajagriha.

3. He died at Kushinagar.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 alone are true: Mahavira preached for 30 years and died at 72 at Pava (Pavapuri) near Rajagriha in the Malla country of Bihar; statement 3 is wrong (महावीर का निर्वाण — पावा, 72 वर्ष)

 

• The notes give his traditional death date as 527 BC, which agrees with a life of 599-527 BC.

 

• Kushinagar is the place where Buddha attained Mahaparinirvana, and the two deaths in Malla territory create the deliberate confusion in statement 3.

 

• Pavapuri has a Jal Mandir (water temple) and the Jain festival of Deepavali is linked to Mahavira's nirvana.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Jain Nirvana era is counted from 527 BC, the traditional year of Mahavira's death.

 

• Mahavira's activity was concentrated in Magadha, Anga, Videha and Kosala.

 

• Buddha died at 80 and Mahavira at 72, a contrast sometimes asked.

 

• Mahavira spent his rainy-season retreats (chaturmasa) at places such as Rajagriha, Vaishali, Nalanda and Pava, and the last rainy season of his life was passed at Pava.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): This combination fails as statement 3 puts Mahavira's death at Kushinagar, which is the Buddha's place of death, and the option also drops the true statement 1.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): Pairing these statements is incorrect since it includes the false statement 3 and leaves out statement 2, which is correct and records the age and place of death.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): That selection cannot hold because statement 3 is false; Mahavira died at Pava (Pavapuri), while Kushinagar is the Buddha's place of Mahaparinirvana.

question: According to the traditional chronology, Mahavira lived during which period?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 599-527 BC.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• According to the traditional timeline in the notes, Mahavira lived from 599 BC to 527 BC, a lifespan of 72 years (महावीर का जीवनकाल — 599-527 ई.पू.)

 

• The notes also record a modern timeline of c. 540-468 BC, which many historians prefer, because it makes him a contemporary of Buddha and of the Magadhan kings Bimbisara and Ajatashatru.

 

• Both timelines give a lifespan of about 72 years, ending with his death at Pava near Rajagriha.

 

• The traditional date is the base of the Jain Vir Nirvana Samvat, the era counted from his death.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Buddha's traditional dates are about 563-483 BC, so on the modern dating the two teachers lived at roughly the same time.

 

• Haryanka rulers Bimbisara and Ajatashatru ruled Magadha in this period, and Jain texts claim Bimbisara (Shrenika) as a sympathiser.

 

• The sixth century BC also saw the rise of the sixteen Mahajanapadas and the second urbanisation of the Ganga plains.

 

NOTE

 

• 563-483 BC (Option 2): 563-483 BC is the traditional dating of Gautama Buddha, a different teacher, who is placed some years after the start of Mahavira's life in the traditional timeline.

 

• 540-468 AD (Option 3): 540-468 AD has the wrong era: the modern timeline of Mahavira is c. 540-468 BC, so this option is a deliberate error in the era.

 

• 322-298 BC (Option 4): 322-298 BC is the reign period of Chandragupta Maurya, the founder of the Mauryan empire, about two centuries after Mahavira's lifetime.

question: The 'Triratna' (Three Gems) of Jainism consist of:
option_1: Right view, right speech, right action
option_3: Right faith, right knowledge, right conduct
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right faith, right knowledge, right conduct.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Triratna (Ratnatraya) of Jainism are Right Faith (Samyak Darshan), Right Knowledge (Samyak Jnana) and Right Conduct (Samyak Charitra), which together form the path to liberation (त्रिरत्न — सम्यक् दर्शन, ज्ञान, चारित्र)

 

• The notes explain right faith as believing in Mahavira's teachings and wisdom, and right conduct as keeping the five great vows.

 

• All three must be followed together: faith without knowledge is blind, knowledge without conduct is useless, and conduct without faith does not free the soul from karma.

 

• Liberation (moksha) means the soul's release from the cycle of birth and death once all karmic matter has been shed.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Buddhism uses the same word Triratna for Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha, which is why this question is often framed as a trap.

 

• The Tattvarthasutra of Umasvati opens with the statement that right faith, knowledge and conduct together constitute the path to liberation.

 

• Jain monks take the five Mahavratas, while lay followers follow the lesser Anuvratas.

 

NOTE

 

• Right view, right speech, right action (Option 1): Right view, right speech and right action are members of the Buddhist Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga) taught by Gautama Buddha, and have nothing to do with the three jewels of Jainism.

 

• Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha (Option 2): Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha are the three jewels of Buddhism, recited in the refuge formula, which is why the word Triratna belongs to both religions and invites confusion.

 

• Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya (Option 4): Ahimsa, Satya and Asteya are three of the five great vows that make up right conduct, which is only one of the three jewels, so they cannot be the full Triratna.

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the Triratnas of Jainism?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right meditation.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Right meditation is not part of the Jain Triratna; the three gems are Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct (सम्यक् ध्यान त्रिरत्न में नहीं है)

 

• 'Right meditation' resembles 'Samma Samadhi' (right concentration), the eighth step of the Buddhist Eightfold Path, and the question mixes up the two religions on purpose.

 

• The notes define the three gems as believing in Mahavira's teachings, accepting the Jain view of soul and world, and keeping the five great vows.

 

• Meditation and austerity do play a part in Jain practice, but they are treated as aids to right conduct and not as a separate jewel.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Buddhist Eightfold Path has eight members: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

 

• Jain tapas (austerity) includes six outer and six inner kinds, among which meditation (dhyana) appears as an inner austerity.

 

• Jainism stresses self-effort, while Buddhism follows the Middle Path between luxury and extreme self-mortification.

 

NOTE

 

• Right faith (Option 2): Right faith (Samyak Darshan) is the first of the three gems, the starting point that gives conviction in the teachings, so it is part of the Triratna and cannot be the answer to a NOT-type question.

 

• Right knowledge (Option 3): Right knowledge (Samyak Jnana) is the second jewel, understanding of the nature of the soul and the world, so it does belong to the Triratna.

 

• Right conduct (Option 4): Right conduct (Samyak Charitra) is the third jewel and consists of the five great vows, so it is a member of the Triratna and cannot be the odd one out.

question: The term 'Samyakcharitra' in Jainism refers to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right conduct.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Samyakcharitra means Right Conduct, the third of the three jewels (Ratnatraya) of Jainism (सम्यक् चारित्र — सही आचरण)

 

• Right conduct is achieved by keeping the five great vows: Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Aparigraha and Brahmacharya, as the notes state.

 

• It is the practical side of the path: the first two jewels give belief and understanding, and this third one turns them into daily discipline.

 

• In Sanskrit 'charitra' means conduct or character, and 'samyak' means right or perfect, which helps in decoding the word.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Samyak Darshan means right faith and Samyak Jnana means right knowledge.

 

• Monks follow Samyakcharitra in its strictest form through the Mahavratas, while householders follow limited vows.

 

• Sallekhana, a voluntary fast unto death, is the final act of right conduct in Jain ethics.

 

• The five Samitis and three Guptis, the rules of careful movement, speech and thought, are the detailed form of right conduct for Jain monks, and they all aim to prevent injury.

 

NOTE

 

• Right faith (Option 1): Right faith is Samyak Darshan, the belief in the teachings of Mahavira, which is the first jewel; it is not the same as Samyakcharitra, which concerns behaviour.

 

• Right meditation (Option 2): Right meditation is not one of the three jewels in Jainism; the phrase is found in the Buddhist Eightfold Path and so is a distractor.

 

• Right knowledge (Option 4): Right knowledge is Samyak Jnana, the second jewel, which covers understanding of soul, matter and karma, and it does not mean conduct.

question:
Match the Jain concept with its meaning:

(a) Samyak Darshan  (i) Right conduct

(b) Samyak Jnana  (ii) Right faith

(c) Samyak Charitra  (iii) Right knowledge

(d) Kevala Jnana  (iv) Supreme or perfect knowledge
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Samyak Darshan - Right faith, Samyak Jnana - Right knowledge, Samyak Charitra - Right conduct and Kevala Jnana - Supreme knowledge give a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (सम्यक् दर्शन = श्रद्धा, सम्यक् ज्ञान, सम्यक् चारित्र, केवल ज्ञान = सर्वोच्च ज्ञान)

 

• The first three together form the Triratna, as the notes state, and the fourth is the result at the end of the spiritual path.

 

• Kevala Gnana is the highest spiritual knowledge, reached by Mahavira in the 13th year of his penance near the Rijupalika river.

 

• Right knowledge means, according to the notes, accepting that the world has always existed without a creator and that every object has a soul.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• A person who attains Kevala Jnana is called a Kevalin, omniscient and free of karmic bondage.

 

• Mahavira attained Kevala Jnana at about 42 and taught for 30 years afterwards.

 

• Jain philosophy lists five kinds of knowledge, of which Kevala Jnana is the highest and the last.

 

• The Tattvarthasutra describes the jewels as the path to liberation, and the seven tattvas, jiva, ajiva, asrava, bandha, samvara, nirjara and moksha, are the Jain categories of reality.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-ii, c-i, d-iv (Option 1): This set swaps right faith and right knowledge, giving Samyak Darshan the meaning of knowledge and Samyak Jnana that of faith, so the first two pairs are reversed.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 3): This set wrongly pairs Samyak Jnana with right conduct and Samyak Charitra with right knowledge, so the second and third jewels are interchanged.

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 4): This set pairs Samyak Darshan with supreme knowledge and Kevala Jnana with right conduct, so three of the four pairs are wrong.
